question: Across all suppliers, did urgent orders in 1996-1997 actually arrive on time more often, and what explains the late ones?

answer.report_markdown:
## Answer
63.4% of line items in scope arrived after the committed date. The strongest factor is dispatch lag (order → ship, days): 01-30d 9.2%, 31-60d 50.9%, 61-90d 91.1%, 91d+ 100%. Ship mode, Supplier region, Order priority were checked and ruled out.

## Supported
- Dispatch lag (order → ship, days): 01-30d 9.2%, 31-60d 50.9%, 61-90d 91.1%, 91d+ 100% — 90.8 pp gap between buckets, p=0.0e+0
- Transit time (ship → receipt, days): 01-10d 55.6%, 11-20d 63.1%, 21-30d 71.4% — 15.8 pp gap between buckets, p=0.0e+0
- Promised window (order → committed date, days): 30-50d 81.5%, 51-70d 62.7%, 71-90d 45% — 36.5 pp gap between buckets, p=0.0e+0

## Ruled out by the Skeptic
- Ship mode: AIR 63.2%, FOB 62.3%, MAIL 64.8%, RAIL 65.4%, REG AIR 64%, SHIP 61.6%, TRUCK 62.9% — only 3.8 pp between best and worst bucket — no meaningful difference
- Supplier region: AFRICA 63.1%, AMERICA 63.8%, ASIA 63.5%, EUROPE 62.8%, MIDDLE EAST 64.1% — only 1.3 pp between best and worst bucket — no meaningful difference
- Order priority: 1-URGENT 61.3%, 2-HIGH 63.7%, 3-MEDIUM 64.9%, 4-NOT SPECIFIED 63.4%, 5-LOW 63.6% — only 3.6 pp between best and worst bucket — no meaningful difference

## Inconclusive
- none

## Recommended actions
- Investigate the dispatch lag (order → ship, days) bucket with the highest late rate first.
- Track this factor weekly so the team sees whether fixes reduce the late rate.
